BOPEN.heard: Sponsor Scout, a final project film by Akshit Verma in four parts.

P1A.heard: International students looking for data jobs have a short clock and only some employers sponsor visas. So we apply to sponsors, but many of them have no entry-level data job open today and those applications go nowhere.

P1B.heard: Sponsor scout tells the student for each sponsor whether to apply, network, check by hand or skip with the public record behind every answer. A strong sponsor with nothing open isn't dropped. It goes on a networking list.

P1C.heard: It never applies emails or contacts anyone. The person decides, I'm building it because I'm job hunting too and I wanted a smarter strategy than a hundred plus applications a day.

P2A.heard: What already exists? My visa jobs list sponsors and their past job counts. I looked at it in October. H1B greater grades employers on past approvals and denials. Interstride, which universities provide, shows sponsorship history and filters jobs by visa.

P2B.heard: The reallocation engine's own scorer, which I had clawed code run in October, gives a sponsor with no open job a zero and skips it. These tools show who sponsored before, or what's open now. None that I found turns a proven sponsor with nothing open into a networking target. That's the gap.

P3A.heard: The data is public, sponsorship records from the 80 days to stay file, recent funding from SEC form defilings, open jobs from the public greenhouse, lever and Ashby job boards. The job seeker is fictional.

P3B.heard: Each sponsor gets three checks, has it sponsored data roles, has it raised money recently, and is an entry-level data job open today. The answers set the verdict. The prototype ran on October 3rd on 123 sponsors.

P3C.heard: but only 16 of them had a known job board, so most answers were checked by hand. So with Claude Code, I built a board resolver. It tries names built from each company's name, one request at a time, saves every raw response with a fingerprint and stops when it's done out of budget or hitting errors.

P3D.heard: It only proposes. I approve or refuse each board, and my decision is tied to the fingerprint of the response I saw. It can only read from those three sites, and it has no way to send anything.

P3E.heard: I have what I need, Claude Code, free public job boards, no keys, and no paid compute. Next, I'll rerun the verdicts on the new boards, then evaluate them.

P4A.heard: How will I know it worked? First, coverage. On November 23rd, the resolver made 629 requests all to the three allowed sites and found candidate boards for 39 companies. After my review, coverage went from 16 to 50 of 123.

P4B.heard: It also got things wrong in ways I could check. Five boards belong to other companies like a childcare center. Claude flagged them and I refused all five. The name check called Wait Watchers a mismatch, though it's the right company. Five approved boards are empty and 67 companies showed no board under the names it tried.

P4C.heard: One bug got passed every test. On a Windows console, the command saved my approval, then crashed. A test now reproduces it, and all 28 tests pass.

P4D.heard: Next, the vertex. Before tuning anything, I'll set aside a hand check set of sponsors. If fewer than 9 in 10 apply vertex are right on that set, it didn't work. And after 14 days, I'll recheck the networking targets for new postings. This sample can show what it gets wrong. It can't show that anyone gets hired.

BOUT.heard: Sponsor Scout, a film by Akshit Verma.
